Three traps. The FSI course, written for American diplomats in 1961, put it in capitals: German and English devices for talking about past time do not coincide exactly.
PASSO 1: o Perfekt é o passado da CONVER: STEP 1: the Perfekt is the past tense of CONVERSATION and messages: «Ich habe Deutsch gelernt». It looks like the English present perfect ("I have learned"), but it does the job of the simple past: «Gestern habe ich gearbeitet» = "I worked yesterday" — English would never say "Yesterday I have worked". STEP 2: it has TWO parts: the auxiliary «haben», conjugated, in 2nd position, and the PARTIZIP II (past participle) at the END of the sentence — the same bracket you know from the modals. STEP 3: the Partizip II of regular verbs is «ge-» + stem + «-t», like English "-ed": machen → gemacht; lernen → gelernt; spielen → gespielt; kaufen → gekauft; kochen → gekocht; hören → gehört. STEP 4: conjugate «haben»: ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie haben. STEP 5: a yes/no question: «Hast du schon gegessen?» (Have you eaten yet? / Did you eat yet?) and the answer: «Ja, schon» or «Nein, noch nicht». STEP 6: use past time words: gestern, letzte Woche, letztes Jahr. And remember the opposite trap: "I've been living here for two years" is NOT a Perfekt in German — it's the present with «seit»: «Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren hier».
o português tem «eu tenho feito» (que nã: English splits the past between "I did" and "I have done", and the choice matters. German conversation uses the Perfekt for both: «Ich habe gegessen» = "I ate" and "I have eaten". The form looks like English (have + participle), but the participle goes to the very END of the sentence.
The Partizip II goes to the END of the sentence — not next to haben as in English.

Casos especiais do Partizip II regular: Special cases of the regular Partizip II
PASSO 1: se a raiz termina em -t ou -d,: STEP 1: if the stem ends in -t or -d, the participle takes «-et» to stay pronounceable — just like English "waited", "needed": arbeiten → gearbeitet; warten → gewartet. STEP 2: verbs in «-ieren» take NO «ge-»: studieren → studiert; telefonieren → telefoniert; reparieren → repariert. These are mostly borrowed words you'll recognize (studieren, reparieren, informieren). STEP 3: verbs with an INSEPARABLE prefix (be-, ge-, er-, ver-, ent-, emp-, zer-) take NO «ge-» either: besuchen → besucht; bezahlen → bezahlt; verkaufen → verkauft; erklären → erklärt. STEP 4: rule of thumb: if the verb starts with be-, er-, ver-, ent- or ge-, or ends in -ieren, its participle has no «ge-». (The FSI's tip: «ge-» only goes on a verb whose FIRST syllable is stressed.)
Stem in -t: the participle takes «-et», like "waited".
The prefix be- already takes the place of «ge-».

Verbos separáveis regulares: o «ge-» vai: Regular separable verbs: «ge-» goes in the middle
PASSO 1: o verbo separável tem prefixo +: STEP 1: a separable verb has prefix + stem: «einkaufen» = ein + kaufen. STEP 2: in the Partizip II, «ge-» goes BETWEEN the prefix and the stem: ein + ge + kauft → «eingekauft»; auf + ge + räumt → «aufgeräumt»; ab + ge + holt → «abgeholt»; an + ge + meldet → «angemeldet» (stem in -d: +et). STEP 3: in the sentence, the whole participle goes to the end: «Ich habe heute eingekauft.» STEP 4: compare with the present: «Ich kaufe heute ein» (prefix at the end) × «Ich habe heute eingekauft» (participle at the end) — "I shop", "I have shopped", with the particle glued back on.
«ge-» goes in the middle, only once.

Two friends talk about the day before.
— Oi, Paul! O que você fez ontem?: — Hi, Paul! What did you do yesterday?
— Trabalhei bastante. Depois fiz compras: — I worked a lot. Then I went shopping.
— Yes, I cooked pasta and listened to music.
— E você já arrumou o apartamento?: — And have you tidied up the apartment yet?

— Que bom! Você a buscou?: — How nice! Did you pick her up?

Trinken forma o Perfekt com haben. Com w: Trinken forms the Perfekt with haben. With wir, use haben: Wir haben Kaffee getrunken.
Kommen forma o Perfekt com sein. Com er,: Kommen forms the Perfekt with sein. With er, the auxiliary is ist: Er ist nach Hause gekommen.
